items.title: Learnings and Pitfalls from AI-Assisted A/B Experimentation at Scale
items.summary:
A/B testing underpins product decisions by providing trustworthy, reproducible quantification of proposed changes' effects. Growing large language model (LLM) capabilities have motivated efforts to automate experimentation workflows. Yet LLMs are nondeterministic and prone to hallucination, properties that conflict with the trust experimentation systems must provide. Experiments are also operationally messy: diagnosing anomalies, debugging configurations, and conducting bespoke follow-up analyses require flexible reasoning and manual effort. These tasks let agents accelerate experimentation without replacing its deterministic statistical foundations.
  We report lessons from building and operating such an agent. Our central finding is that this tension is resolved not by making the model deterministic, but by bounding where its nondeterminism can reach; the model selects and sequences procedures, while deterministic code computes every quantity it reports. Three consequences surprised us: withholding information from the model improved its answers, demand concentrated on mundane retrieval rather than the autonomous decisions we anticipated, and the agent's eagerness to help threatened statistical validity.

items.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.

items.title: Heads That Write, Not Just Point: Image Retrieval Heads in Vision-Language Models
items.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: https://github.com/parkquasar/Image-Retrieval-Heads.

items.title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
items.story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put it his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. items.title: See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
items.summary: Personal AI agents have changed how users interact with the web, blurring the lines between automated and human traffic. Learn how Cloudflare gives site owners visibility and control to manage personal agent access.
items.story_key: story|title:see the agents set the terms new visibility and control for personal agents
items.content_excerpt: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. items.title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
items.summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

items.title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.

items.title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
items.summary: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the \textit{locality hypothesis}, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a \textit{Discover-Trace-Realign} paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate-wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off. items.title: Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM
items.summary: Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell.
items.story_key: model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0 support for mistral large 4 on vllm
items.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . items.title: claude-code v2.1.317
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
  • Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume
  • Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
  • Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
  • Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
  • [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when chat.fontSize is raised
  • [VSCode] Fixed ultrathink not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart claude remote-control, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
  • [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel
release_highlights: Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run

items.title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.177
items.summary:
New Features

  • on_failure option for HookMatcher: Control what happens when a hook callback fails. Set on_failure="block" to block the action when a callback raises, returns None, or returns a value the CLI rejects. Defaults to "continue" (treat failure as no decision). Requires a CLI version that supports this option; connecting to an older CLI with on_failure="block" raises CLIConnectionError (#1460)

Internal/Other Changes

  • Updated bundled Claude CLI to version 2.1.317
  • Tests: e2e tests now accept either Bash or PowerShell tool in shell-dependent tests, fixing intermittent failures on Windows (#1467)

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/claude-agent-sdk/0.2.177/

pip install claude-agent-sdk==0.2.177
